They are then stuck, because they lack the knowledge and budget to build and run the production ML pipeline properly, the infra stack necessary to handle production workload. comments.text:
This is interesting. For a long time it was pointed out that ZIP codes, unlike say, city or state boundaries, were not properly representable as polygons, since they don't divide up acreage into zones, but rather label postal delivery routes. Suppose I build a new neighborhood way out in the middle of nowhere. The "polygon" concept suggests that we could look and see what polygon I'm in, and that will determine what post office delivers my mail. But in reality, if there was no route to that area already, they could decide to make it part of any one of the surrounding routes.
I suppose though, as long as you let the polygons map has uncontained areas, where no routes currently exist, it's a doable task to draw polygons around the limits of every route network, as long as you don't mind that they may have lots of weird ragged edges.

stories.title_en: Locating the source of a mysterious beep

comments.author: chimpontherun
comments.text:
Around '05 or so, the house we were staying in started beeping.  Smoke alarm sounds, as usual.  For almost a day we couldn't find the source.  Contacted the owners -- they didn't know it either.  They bought the house few years prior, so not much of a help.
Standing in the hallways listening at different angles, as the article says, didn't help.  No Fable in '05 either.
So I had to improvise.  Got a ~1 meter stick and two headphones (every headphone is a microphone, even if it sucks as a microphone).  Plugged them into the stereo mic port, and started recording in Audacity.  The phase shift between L and R pointed directly to the source.  Took about 4 or 5 beeps to get the sucker.
Turns out, it was hiding above the ceiling tiles in the garage.  My wife still tells this story to all her friends as one of my biggest life achievements.  Everything I shipped, the companies I founded -- pales in comparison to finding a dead smoke alarm

comments.author: LoganDark
comments.text: Whitespace depends on the context. For example, you could have characters that are not counted as whitespace in Unicode, but end up rendering as whitespace when displayed in a particular context. The only real way to check for this is to actually try to render it and see what happens. There are some other ways to approximate it, like checking the font that you use for rendering, or the bounds of the glyph, or other things like that, but the only way to really know for sure in all cases is just to render it and see what happens.

comments.author: miki123211

On that note: I was always wondering whether you could do stupid CT log tricks.
If I remember correctly, Let's Encrypt lets you go up to a hundred domains per certificate, with 256 characters per domain[1]. If you get a short domain like a.bc and start requesting certificates for its subdomains, you can easily get a few kB of user-controlled data embeddable per certificate. Given LE's rate limits, it should, within a few weeks of easily-automated work, be possible to embed child pornography into a CT log, making it illegal to host and destroying it completely.
You could do something more useful (and less destructive) with this idea; like embedding a separate public key, with the corresponding private key stored offline in an HSM, which could then be used to sign the location of your new domain in case the old one was seized. This would, in a weird and perverted way, add a lot more censorship resistance to DNS than what it natively provides.
You could even use a CT log as a blockchain, with the order of log entries being used for consensus.

I think the novel thing here, that I have not yet seen in any other database app, is the realization that normal SQL joins are not quite what you want in most cases.
Often, you are interested in nested results. "Give me all my customers with a list of their orders." I'm a fan of the 'sandwich' model: someone needs to say what to do, someone needs to do it, and someone needs to say if it's been done [well enough]. "one-shotting" is fun for a low (human) effort toy, but it's a mistake to get overly hung up on LLMs getting everything right on the first try, since a lot of that is the harness and the internal prompting that makes it burn extra tokens to test everything to get it in that one "shot" (ui turn).
While it's nice that LLMs are getting better at arriving at the desired deliverable with fewer surprises (or broken things) doing it is not necessarily a sign that the model is actually smarter, just an indication that what you are doing is likely a well-trodden path for the model, the RL and the harness.
